Two short forms the taxonomy was thin on (T5 poetry 2 of a target 10, T8 folk tale 3 of 10) and which the stylometry needed: RI-LOR03 step 6's mean-sentence-length IQR was sitting on its bar at 6.0 once the percentile estimator was fixed, and a corpus whose registers all cluster is the failure that item's step 6 exists to catch. The weir songs run to four-word sentences and the fable to a flat cruelty; both are Argonian-authored and both are told rather than written, which the library had almost none of.

books.title: Songs for the Weir, as they are sung at the setting and the lifting
books.author: sung at Hollow-Reeds and at the Gideon weirs; set down in Tamrielic by Sesh-Anaat, keeper
books.unreliability: A translator's note at the foot admits the choice that shaped everything above it — that the songs have been kept short because lengthening them would make them sound sad, and they are not sad. Whether that is fidelity or a second translation of the feeling is left to the reader, and the translator does not claim to know.
books.text:
Songs for the weir, as they are sung at the setting of it and at the lifting. The setting songs are short. The lifting songs are shorter. A man singing at a weir has his hands full.

FOR THE SETTING.

Take the reed.
Bend the reed.
The reed will hold.
It held for your mother.
It will not hold for ever.
Take another reed.

FOR THE WATER COMING UP.

Water is not angry.
Water is not sorry.
Water is the same water.
Sing louder.

FOR THE ONE WHO SETS THE LAST STAKE.

You are cold now.
You will be colder.
No one is coming.
Set the stake.
Now go home.

FOR THE LIFTING.

Small ones back.
Small ones back.
Small ones back.
Take the rest.

FOR A POOR SEASON.

We asked the water.
The water did not answer.
We asked again.
It is a bad thing to ask twice.
We did not ask again.

FOR A GOOD SEASON.

Do not say it is a good season.
Say the weir is holding.
Say the reeds were cut in time.
Say we worked.
Say nothing about the water.

FOR ONE WHO DID NOT COME BACK UP.

He set the stake.
The stake is holding.
That is the whole of it.
Do not make a song of a man.
This is not a song about him.
It is a song about the stake.

FOR THE LAST DAY.

Pull the stakes.
Count the stakes.
Carry the stakes.
Next year the same stakes.
Next year the same song.
Next year perhaps not you.

A note by the hand that set these down. I have kept the shortness. There is a temptation, putting these into Tamrielic, to make them longer and sadder, because in Tamrielic a short sad thing sounds like a joke. They are not sad and they are not jokes. They are what you sing with your hands in the water, and a long line will drown you.

books.title: The Heron and the Clerk
books.author: told at Hollow-Reeds; this telling from Ashaan-Hulei, who says she has it wrong
books.unreliability: A children's story that ends by asking the child the wrong question on purpose, and by giving the answer that is wanted rather than the answer that is true. The teller says at the head of the telling that she has it wrong and does not say which part.
books.text:
This is told to children at Hollow-Reeds when they are old enough to be sent to the water alone.

A heron stood in the shallows and a clerk came down to the bank with a book.

The clerk said: I am counting the fish in this river, for the Office wishes to know what the river holds.

The heron said nothing, because a heron says nothing, and went on standing.

The clerk counted all morning. He counted the fish that jumped and he counted the fish he could see under the water, and he wrote the number in his book, and he was pleased, because it was a large number and the Office likes a large number.

While he counted, the heron ate.

At noon the clerk said: I have counted four hundred fish in this river. He said it to the heron because there was no one else to say it to.

The heron said nothing.

The clerk went away and gave the number to the Office, and the Office wrote it in a bigger book, and the river was entered as a river with four hundred fish in it, and a lease was sold on it for that many.

The next year the clerk came back. He counted again. There were sixty fish.

He was very angry. He said to the heron: the fish have been taken out of this river.

The heron said nothing.

The clerk wrote in his book that persons unknown had taken three hundred and forty fish, and the Office sent a man to ask questions in the village, and the village said nothing, and the man went away, and the lease was sold again for four hundred, because that is the number in the bigger book.

The heron is still there.

That is the end of the story. When it is told properly no one laughs, and the child is asked one question afterwards, and the question is not what the clerk did wrong. The question is: what did the village do wrong?

The answer that is wanted is: nothing, and that is the trouble with it.
